newsitem.title: BRAZIL: S&P to review Brazil credit rating next month.
newsitem.headline: S&P to review Brazil credit rating next month.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp's rating committee could meet as early as next month to review its B-plus sovereign credit rating for Brazil, S&P President Leo C. O'Neill said.

"Our rating committee will be meeting over the next month or so to review this position we have on Brazil and at that point we will either affirm the rating or potentially raise it," O'Neill told reporters at a news conference to announce a new partnership with Brazilian economic think-tank Getulio Vargas Foundation.
S&P currently has a positive outlook on its B-plus rating for Brazil, indicating it is more likely to be upgraded than downgraded.

Brazil received a single-B rating from S&P in November 1994, just four months after the launch of a tough anti-inflation drive known as the Real Plan. The plan, which proved successful at slashing inflation and stabilizing the Brazilian economy, was a key reason behind S&P's decision to upgrade Brazil in July 1995 to B-plus.
Brazil, however, still trails its neighbors in the credit risk category. S&P rates Chile's sovereign credit risk at A-minus, Mexico's at BB and Argentina at BB-minus.
O'Neill, who is also S&P's chief rating officer, said Brazil's total public debt to gross domestic product ratio of about 34 percent was much higher than the other large Latin American countries.
He added that Brazil has also been slower in opening its economy than its neighbors and that it needed to make steadier progress to cut its fiscal deficit.

"Even if we were to upgrade Brazil, we would not upgrade to the investment-grade category. These upgrades and downgrades tend to occur in much smaller steps," O'Neill said, adding that Brazil, if raised, would probably wind up with a BB-minus rating, the next notch up from B-plus.
The lowest investment-grade level is BBB-minus, four levels above Brazil's current B-plus rating.
Brazilian officials have argued for a credit upgrade for over a year, saying Brazilian debt has traded in the secondary market at spreads equal to or tighter than Mexican and Argentine spreads.
